title: Explain the structural patterns Adapter, Decorator, Composite, Proxy, Facade, Bridge, and Flyweight.
shortTitle: Explain the structural patterns Adapter, Decorator, Composite, Proxy, Facade, Bridge, and Flyweight
keyPoints: Adapter converts one interface into another so incompatible types can work together, used for legacy or third-party integration.
Decorator adds behaviour at runtime by wrapping an object that shares the same interface, avoiding subclass explosion.
Composite treats individual objects and groups uniformly through a tree structure, used for portfolios and account groups.
Proxy controls access to a real object by adding lazy creation, security checks, or caching behind the same interface.
Facade provides one simple entry point over a complex subsystem, hiding internal interactions from the client.
Bridge separates abstraction from implementation so both can vary independently, avoiding a class explosion.
Adapter changes the interface, Decorator adds behaviour with the same interface, and Proxy controls access with the same interface.

s1_definition.oneliner: Adapter converts, Decorator wraps to add, Composite forms trees, Proxy controls access, Facade simplifies, Bridge splits abstraction from implementation, and Flyweight shares to save memory.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Adapter** – converts one interface into another so incompatible types can work together, used to integrate legacy or third-party code.
- **Decorator** – adds behaviour to an object at runtime by wrapping it in another object that implements the same interface.
- **Composite** – treats individual objects and groups of objects uniformly through a tree structure.
- **Proxy** – stands in for another object to control access, adding lazy creation, security, or caching.
- **Facade** – provides one simple front to a complex subsystem, hiding interactions.
- **Bridge** – separates an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently.
- **Flyweight** – shares common immutable state across many objects to save memory.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India: an Adapter is the converter that lets the new app talk to the old mainframe. A Decorator is adding gift wrapping to a parcel layer by layer without changing the parcel. A Composite is a folder of accounts that contains both single accounts and sub-folders, all totalled the same way. A Proxy is the security guard who checks your ID before letting you reach the manager. A Facade is the single help desk that hides all the back departments. A Bridge is a remote control whose buttons stay the same while the device behind it can change.

```text
  Proxy:     Client ──→ [Proxy] ──→ Real (same interface, controls)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Structural patterns are about how you compose classes and objects into larger structures while keeping them flexible. Adapter converts one interface into another so incompatible types work together, which is how Rajesh wraps a legacy ledger behind a clean `LedgerPort`. Decorator adds behaviour at runtime by wrapping an object that shares the same interface, so logging, encryption, and SMS can be stacked in any order without subclass explosion. Composite treats single objects and groups uniformly through a tree, which is how a portfolio totals its value whether a node is a holding or a sub-portfolio.

Proxy provides a stand-in that controls access to the real object, adding security checks or lazy loading, which is exactly how Spring's transactional proxy wraps a bean. Facade gives one simple entry point over a complicated subsystem, so a client calls a single transfer method instead of orchestrating validation, fees, ledger posting, and notification. Bridge separates abstraction from implementation so the two can vary independently, letting any account type combine with any interest engine. And Flyweight shares common immutable state across many objects to save memory, which is how millions of trades reuse one interned currency object.

The critical distinction is that Adapter, Decorator, and Proxy all wrap an object, but their intent is different. Adapter changes the interface, Decorator adds behaviour while keeping the same interface, and Proxy controls access while keeping the same interface. Naming the intent, not just the structure, is what shows real understanding.

In the account and notification subsystem at National Bank of India, these appear together naturally: an Adapter bridges the old ledger, Decorators layer logging and encryption on notifications, a Composite totals Rajesh's nested portfolio, a Proxy enforces authorisation on balance reads, and a Facade exposes a single clean transfer call.

Remember one sentence: structural patterns compose objects into larger structures, and the difference between Adapter, Decorator, and Proxy is intent: convert, add, or control.
